column2: A manager can delegate decision authority for a task while retaining accountability to the manager's own superior; responsibility assigned to a subordinate does not erase that upward accountability.
column3: Assigning the task and authority transfers all of the manager's accountability to the subordinate.

column2: Giving a supervisor responsibility for delivery without sufficient scheduling authority can create a mismatch; merely increasing the performance target does not correct that authority gap.
column3: Higher assigned responsibility automatically creates all necessary formal authority even if decision rights remain with another manager.

column2: A firm may delegate routine decisions while retaining strategic decisions centrally; delegation at one level does not prove that the entire organisation is decentralised.
column3: Delegating any routine decision makes every strategic decision decentralised by definition.

column2: A product-divisional structure can improve product accountability while duplicating functions across divisions; a functional structure groups specialist activities across products.
column3: A product-divisional structure necessarily eliminates duplicated specialist functions because each product has its own manager.

column2: A matrix combines reporting dimensions, potentially improving coordination while creating dual-authority conflicts; clear decision rules are needed rather than assuming unity of command is automatically preserved.
column3: A matrix guarantees single-supervisor unity of command because each employee belongs to only one specialist profession.

column2: Task standardisation, staff competence and coordination needs affect a workable supervisory span; one universal span need not fit routine and highly interdependent work equally.
column3: A wider span always reduces coordination difficulty because it removes managerial levels regardless of task interdependence.

column2: Control compares outcomes with standards and can feed corrective information into future planning; establishing a standard without measuring performance does not complete the control cycle.
column3: Control is completed when the plan is approved because future measurements cannot alter already established standards.

column2: Participative goal setting and periodic review can align individual and organisational goals; poorly specified measures can still induce goal displacement.
column3: An MBO system prevents goal displacement even if employees are rewarded exclusively for an incomplete numerical indicator.

column2: Under Herzberg's account, removing poor working-condition dissatisfaction is distinguished from creating motivation through achievement, recognition and the work itself.
column3: Improving a hygiene factor necessarily creates the same motivational effect as increased achievement and responsibility under Herzberg's model.

column2: An expectancy account requires perceived effort-performance linkage, performance-reward linkage and reward value; a valued reward can still motivate weakly when employees distrust the linkage.
column3: High reward value alone ensures high motivation even when employees believe performance has no effect on reward.

column2: Perceived inequity concerns an employee's input-outcome ratio relative to a referent, so equal pay can still seem inequitable when perceived inputs differ.
column3: Equal absolute pay necessarily establishes perceived equity irrespective of effort, skill or the employee's comparison referent.

column2: McGregor's contrasting managerial assumptions can influence control practices; Theory Y does not imply that coordination and performance accountability are unnecessary.
column3: Theory Y requires abandoning all performance accountability because employees are assumed capable of self-direction.

column2: Removing an aversive condition when desired behaviour occurs is negative reinforcement; imposing an aversive consequence to reduce behaviour is punishment.
column3: Removing an aversive condition to increase desired behaviour is punishment because the reinforcement is called negative.

column2: Contingency approaches examine the fit between leadership and the situation rather than prescribing an identical degree of direction for every team's readiness and task.
column3: Contingency leadership identifies one universally best behavioural style independent of task and follower conditions.

column2: Inspiring a shared vision and challenging assumptions illustrates transformational behaviour; contingent reward for agreed performance illustrates transactional behaviour, and both can coexist.
column3: Using contingent rewards rules out transformational leadership in the same leader because the two behaviours cannot coexist.

column2: High cohesion combined with suppression of dissent can impair evaluation; structured challenge and independent input can improve scrutiny without requiring hostility.
column3: High cohesion guarantees accurate decisions because disagreement is the principal source of factual error.

column2: Overemphasising personal disposition and discounting situational constraints when judging another person's behaviour illustrates fundamental attribution error.
column3: Explaining another person's failure mainly by situational constraints while discounting disposition is fundamental attribution error.

column2: Allowing one favourable trait to dominate all performance dimensions is halo error; over-weighting the latest events in the review period is recency error.
column3: A supervisor rating every dimension highly because of one strong presentation exhibits recency error even without any emphasis on recent timing.

column2: Job analysis identifies duties and requirements, while job evaluation assesses relative job worth for pay design; employee performance appraisal is a separate assessment.
column3: Job evaluation measures how well a particular employee performed last quarter rather than the job's relative worth.

column2: An assessment can produce consistent scores and still fail to predict the job criterion; reliability alone does not establish selection validity.
column3: A highly reliable test must be valid for hiring any role because consistent measurement establishes job relevance.

column2: A selection tool's usefulness depends on job-related predictive evidence and decision context; face plausibility alone is insufficient evidence of criterion-related validity.
column3: A test that appears appropriate to managers has established predictive validity even when no relationship with later performance has been examined.

column2: Separating organisational, task and person needs helps distinguish a skill deficit from problems caused by resources or incentives; training need not fix every performance gap.
column3: Every performance gap establishes a training need even when workers know the task but lack the required equipment.

column2: Positive trainee reactions do not by themselves establish workplace behaviour change or improved business outcomes; evaluation should match the intended outcome.
column3: A high satisfaction score proves the training improved organisational results without any behaviour or outcome measurement.

column2: Succession planning develops a longer-term talent pipeline and readiness for future roles; merely naming an emergency substitute does not complete that development process.
column3: An emergency replacement list alone constitutes a complete succession-development programme even if no candidates receive preparation.

column2: Multiple perspectives can broaden feedback while retaining source bias and implementation risks; combining raters does not automatically make the result objective.
column3: A 360-degree score is bias-free because self, peers and supervisors jointly rate the employee.

column2: Rewarding only individual output can discourage cooperation when work is interdependent; the incentive measure should reflect the behaviour and outcomes required.
column3: An individual-output incentive automatically maximises team cooperation because each worker's output contributes to the total.

column2: Collective bargaining concerns negotiation between representative parties, while worker participation concerns involvement in relevant management decisions; the two mechanisms can coexist.
column3: Worker participation automatically replaces every collective bargaining process because consultation and negotiation are identical.

column2: Expert power stems from valued competence, while legitimate power stems from recognised role authority; losing a formal title need not remove the person's expert influence.
column3: Expert power ceases immediately when formal authority is removed because expertise and legitimate position are the same power base.

column2: Compromise involves mutual concessions, while collaboration seeks a solution addressing underlying interests; a quick split of differences does not necessarily solve the underlying cause.
column3: Splitting the difference is collaboration by definition because both parties concede an equal amount.

column2: Formal adoption of an ethics policy does not establish an ethical culture when incentives reward violations; sustained change requires consistency among systems, leadership and behaviour.
column3: Publishing an ethics policy establishes an ethical culture regardless of incentives and leaders' observed conduct.
